problem.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ be positive real numbers which satisfy the system of equations $$(a+b)(c+d) = 143,$$ $$(a+c)(b+d) = 150,$$ $$(a+d)(b+c) = 169.$$ Find the smallest possible value of $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2$.

steps.title: Where to start: squares from a squared sum
steps.body:
Let $S = a + b + c + d$ and let $P = ab + ac + ad + bc + bd + cd$ be the sum of all six pairwise products. Squaring $S$ gives every square once and every pairwise product twice, so
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = S^2 - 2P.$$
The given equations are products of two sums, and expanding them produces exactly pairwise products, which is why this identity is the right tool.

steps.title: Add the three equations
steps.body: In the same way, $(a+c)(b+d) = ab + ad + bc + cd$ and $(a+d)(b+c) = ab + ac + bd + cd$. Across the three expansions, each of the six pairwise products appears exactly twice, so adding them gives $2P = 143 + 150 + 169 = 462$. So $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = S^2 - 462$, and we need the smallest possible $S^2$.

your_turn.prompt: In each given equation, the two factors add up to the same thing. What is it?
your_turn.answer: $S$. For example $(a + b) + (c + d) = a + b + c + d$.

steps.title: Bound $S$ with AM-GM
steps.body: AM-GM says two positive numbers with product $Q$ have sum at least $2\sqrt{Q}$, with equality only when the two numbers are equal. Applied to each equation this gives $S^2 \ge 4\cdot 143 = 572$, $S^2 \ge 4\cdot 150 = 600$ and $S^2 \ge 4\cdot 169 = 676$. All three must hold at once, so $S^2 \ge 676$.

your_turn.prompt: For $S^2 = 676$ we need equality in the third bound. What does that force?
your_turn.answer: $a + d = b + c$, and since their product is $169$, both equal $13$ (so $S = 26$).

steps.title: Check that $S = 26$ really happens
steps.body: Careful: a lower bound is only the minimum if some positive $a, b, c, d$ reach it. With $S = 26$, the numbers $a + b$ and $c + d$ add to $26$ and multiply to $143$, and $a + c$ and $b + d$ add to $26$ and multiply to $150$. Choosing $a + b = 13 + \sqrt{26}$, $a + c = 13 + \sqrt{19}$ and $a + d = 13$ gives $a = \tfrac{13 + \sqrt{26} + \sqrt{19}}{2}$, $b = \tfrac{13 + \sqrt{26} - \sqrt{19}}{2}$, $c = \tfrac{13 - \sqrt{26} + \sqrt{19}}{2}$, $d = \tfrac{13 - \sqrt{26} - \sqrt{19}}{2}$.

your_turn.prompt: Why are $a + b$ and $c + d$ equal to $13 \pm \sqrt{26}$? And is $d$ positive?
your_turn.answer: They are the roots of $t^2 - 26t + 143 = 0$, which are $13 \pm \sqrt{26}$. And $\sqrt{26} + \sqrt{19} < 5.2 + 4.4 = 9.6 < 13$, so $d > 0$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: These positive values satisfy all three equations, since $(13 + \sqrt{26})(13 - \sqrt{26}) = 143$, $(13 + \sqrt{19})(13 - \sqrt{19}) = 150$ and $13 \cdot 13 = 169$. So the smallest possible $S^2$ is $676$, and the smallest value of $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2$ is $676 - 462 = 214$. The answer is **$214$**.
